_: The table declarations. This is data: the installer recognises none of the names below. docs/tables.md is the authority on the shape.

tables.name: handle
tables._: One row = one callable thing. The database holds only the name; the real function lives in the in-process registry. This row is what tells the kernel such a function exists.

columns.name: name
columns._: fn: runs inside the kernel process; http:// runs in another process

columns.name: expect_ms
columns._: How long it is expected to take; past this it is declared dead. Same rule inside and out

columns.name: module
columns._: Where an fn: implementation comes from: `path#exportName`. Empty = shipped with the binary (the ones registered in code). Out-of-process handles do not use this column

tables.name: api
tables._: A row is defined by which environment variable holds the key, plus the model to call. Secrets never enter the database.

columns.name: handle
columns._: → handle.name

columns.name: modes
columns._: Its values are registered in the mode table

columns.name: base_url
columns._: Where the calls go. In the table, not in the code: an address that lives only in code cannot be seen in a snapshot, and one that lives in an environment variable cannot be seen at all. Point a row somewhere else and that row goes somewhere else

columns.name: retry_on
columns._: Which failures are worth trying again, as a JSON list of HTTP status codes plus the word network for a call that never got a reply. Anything not listed is returned as it is - a 400 says the request itself was wrong, and sending it again only spends the clock to fail the same way. Which failures are transient differs per key and per model, so it lives on this row rather than in code

columns.name: compress_at
columns._: How many tokens of context this row tolerates before the context is compressed on the way out. Empty = never; the messages go as they are. It belongs to the row and not to the code because the ceiling is a property of this key and this model: one measured run put 1033906 tokens on the wire against a limit of 1048576, and the three stations that went over were over by 738, 1714 and 4150 - a margin, not a runaway. The engine has no tokenizer, so it counts the bytes it is about to send and divides: 4234989 bytes measured against a reported 1033906 tokens, so 4 bytes to a token

tables.name: mode
tables._: Registers which api modes exist.

tables.name: cycle
tables._: The cycle table. One row = one cycle within one mode. This is what the kernel advances on.

columns.name: mode
columns._: 1 which mode

columns.name: cycle
columns._: 2 which cycle within that mode

columns.name: api_mode
columns._: Which api mode this cycle needs (chat / duplex / ...). Empty = this station uses no model and goes through agent.unit

columns.name: must_call
columns._: The one tool this station has to call. Empty = it picks for itself. Set, and the call goes out with that tool forced, so the station cannot end without it. Note that some vendors refuse a forced choice while their thinking mode is on

columns.name: max_units
columns._: 3 how many execution units are allowed

columns.name: from
columns._: 4 which rows it usually comes from. A JSON list

columns.name: next
columns._: 5 which rows usually come next. A JSON list

columns.name: infer
columns._: 6 the inference function -> handle.name. Columns 4 and 5 decide it

tables.name: task
tables._: The task table. One row = the head node of one task.

columns.name: mode
columns._: -> cycle.mode, which also decides which sub-table holds the detail

columns.name: place
columns._: → workplace.place

columns.name: run
columns._: What this run is called. One bench is a batch of tasks, identified by this. Empty = belongs to no run

columns.name: source
columns._: Who published it: user / agent / world / eacn. This is an admission criterion, not metadata

columns.name: domain
columns._: Which kind of problem this is (physics / chem / coding ...). Extensions are dispatched on it: a skill / tool / rule states its applicability as a dim=task,key=domain term. It does not belong in mode: mode is the reasoning mechanism (cot / tot / tree), which is a different axis from what field the problem is in. Empty = unclassified

columns.name: description
columns._: The task description in natural language. Transparent to the kernel; how to read it is the agent's business

columns.name: created_at
columns._: Wall-clock creation time; metadata

columns.name: workdir
columns._: The landing path inside that place. Empty = the cwd on that machine

columns.name: objective
columns._: Whether this task has a grading function. The definition is not here: it is in the sealed store, out of reach of the API

columns.name: readable
columns._: A policy bit: whether the definition of the grading function may be read directly. If a task carries one, this must be given explicitly; there is no default

columns.name: claimed_by
columns._: The current holder. Empty = unclaimed

columns.name: result
columns._: The wrap-up result. Only present once done or failed

columns.name: max_branches
columns._: How many branches may be open at once

columns.name: max_dead_siblings
columns._: How many dead siblings under one parent before backtracking a level to change direction

columns.name: solve_seconds
columns._: Upper bound on solving time, in seconds

columns.name: max_searches
columns._: How many searches one attempt gets. Null or absent means no limit. Counted per attempt the way the grading function's checks are - a fresh attempt gets a fresh allowance - and a refused call costs nothing, because nothing was looked up. It exists because searching spends the clock, not the unit budget: in one measured run the timed-out tasks put about half their hour into it while never coming close to their per-station cap, so the limit that binds has to be on searches themselves.

columns.name: no_search
columns._: A JSON list of strings the publisher forbids searching around. If any of them turns up ANYWHERE in what a search brings back - the prose, the queries it ran, the pages it opened - the whole result is dropped and the caller is told the publisher does not allow it. Empty or absent means no restriction. It exists because a graded problem usually has its answer published somewhere: one measured run went after the dataset itself by name, and when the front door did not open it tried a mirror, then a text-extraction proxy, then the Internet Archive - all with queries like 'row 1 answer'. Blocking by URL alone does not hold, which is why the check is on the whole payload, and why it happens before the model ever sees it: once an answer is in the context the problem is already spent, and voiding it afterwards only records the loss.

columns.name: state
columns._: Where it stands: open / claimed / done / failed. Derived from the sub-table, then written back

tables.name: agent
tables._: One row = one agent (an agent card, unpacked).

columns.name: config
columns._: Where its config file is

columns.name: apis
columns._: A JSON list; each entry is [key_env, model]

columns.name: unit
columns._: The execution-unit handle -> handle.name

columns.name: knobs
columns._: Model settings this agent always calls with, as a JSON object; whatever it does not name falls back to the run-wide config. It belongs on the agent because it is a property of the agent, not of the run: a searcher that reads and reports wants no reasoning at all, while the solver it answers to wants as much as it can afford, and one dial cannot be both. Measured, the difference is not small - the same question took 14.5s at none and 113s at low, and the 98 seconds bought ten thousand tokens of reasoning about which paper it was, which is not what a searcher is for. Without this column, turning the solver's reasoning up would silently make every search eight times slower, and nothing would say why.

tables.name: workplace
tables._: Registers the places where work happens. Not a lookup table.

columns.name: place
columns._: A layered address string

columns.name: identity
columns._: The handle that resolves this address and forwards tool calls there -> handle.name. Required whenever forward is on; empty otherwise

columns.name: runtime
columns._: The runtime shipped over when the connection is made (a local file path). Empty for local

columns.name: forward
columns._: Whether tools are forwarded there

columns.name: tools
columns._: The allow-list. A JSON list; each entry carries a policy

columns.name: usable
columns._: Registered availability, not a liveness probe

tables.name: rule
tables._: Rules. They may be registered from outside, and rows appear at any time.

columns.name: identity
columns._: → handle.name

columns.name: params
columns._: JSON

columns.name: writes
columns._: Declares which tables it writes and how. JSON

columns.name: access
columns._: How an external rule reaches the database. JSON; secrets are stored only as environment variable names

columns.name: scope
columns._: Which rows it may touch. A structured match expression, not a SQL fragment

tables.name: trigger
tables._: When my turn comes. Shared by rule / skill / tool. One row = one term.

columns.name: group
columns._: AND within a group, OR across groups

columns.name: dim
columns._: agent / task / cycle / chain

columns.name: key
columns._: Empty string for the chain dimension

tables.name: tool
tables._: One row = one tool. name is what the model sees, and what the workplace allow-list references.

columns.name: identity
columns._: → handle.name

columns.name: does
columns._: The description the model reads

columns.name: params
columns._: The argument schema the model reads

columns.name: output
columns._: The result schema, also read by the model

columns.name: prompt
columns._: A usage convention this tool adds to the system instructions

columns.name: concurrent
columns._: Whether it may run alongside other tools

columns.name: system
columns._: A system tool: every agent has it from the start, with no trigger lookup

columns.name: gives
columns._: -> msg_part.name: what kind of thing its result is, so that compressing a context knows what it may throw away. look is a state that can be looked at again and that goes stale - a file read is the file as it was, and once the same file has been edited the copy is worse than nothing. event is something that happened and cannot be had back - a test run that took four minutes, a verdict. receipt is the line that says a change went through. Empty = event, because assuming a thing can be had again when it cannot is the one direction that loses what nobody can get back

tables.name: skill
tables._: One row = one skill. The model does not pick it; it is injected when its terms match.

columns.name: identity
columns._: → handle.name

columns.name: body
columns._: Empty for dynamically generated ones; the handle produces the content on demand

tables.name: mcp_server
tables._: Registers one MCP server. Its tools are not written here: once connected it reports them through tools/list, and each grows one row in tool.

columns.name: name
columns._: Its name. Handle names are mcp:<name>/<tool>, so it must not contain a /

columns.name: spec
columns._: How to start it. JSON, the same shape as an MCP client config: {command,args,env} or {url,headers}. Secrets are stored only as environment variable names

tables.name: msg_role
tables._: Registers message roles, and where each one goes on the way out. This is the only place that says it: the same kind can wear two roles (the world injects one as user, the kernel injects one as system), so where a line goes cannot be read off its kind.

columns.name: sent_as
columns._: messages = a line in the conversation. instructions = part of what this turn is told, resent every turn and not a thing anyone said

tables.name: msg_kind
tables._: Registers message kinds. Adding one = adding a row; no other table changes.

tables.name: press_how
tables._: Registers what can be done to a part of a message when the context is compressed, and who does it. A row here is a name the l1/l2/l3 columns of msg_part are allowed to hold - a value that is not registered is a typo that would otherwise silently do nothing. Shaped like the tool table on purpose: a name, the handle that runs it, and the two schemas. So the ones that ship in the binary and the ones declared over HTTP are the same kind of row, and a way of pressing that needs a model - or a machine that is not this one - is declared, not coded in.

columns.name: identity
columns._: -> handle.name: who actually does it. fn: runs inside this process, http:// runs somewhere else. Empty = the way is registered but nothing implements it here; asking for it is an error at press time rather than a silent pass-through

columns.name: params
columns._: What the handle is given, as a JSON schema. The same shape for every way: which part it is, the text of it, how big, which level asked. Declared rather than assumed, because an outside implementation has no way to read our minds and every mismatch here is a wrong context that still looks like a context

columns.name: output
columns._: What the handle answers, as a JSON schema: the text that stands in, or nothing at all for a way that drops. A way that answers something else is refused at press time - a compressed context that quietly became the string undefined is the worst of the failures, because it still sends

tables.name: msg_part
tables._: One row = one kind of thing a message carries, and what happens to it at each level. A message row is not one lump: an assistant row holds the reasoning (its own column), what it said, and the calls it asked for, and those three are worth keeping to very different degrees - one measured run had 143 MB of reasoning against 1.7 MB of speech. The kernel writes down which parts a row has and how big they are; which of them survives a level is this table's business, so that no tool name and no policy ever lands in kernel code.

columns.name: name
columns._: What this part is. A part is recognised from the shape a message already has to carry (deliver.ts checks it on the way in), never from what a tool means

columns.name: l1
columns._: -> press_how.name: what happens to this part at the lightest level

columns.name: l2
columns._: -> press_how.name

columns.name: l3
columns._: -> press_how.name: the heaviest of the levels that are set up

columns.name: l4
columns._: -> press_how.name: the fourth level, and the only one that may be empty. Empty anywhere in this column means the level is not set up: nothing is written for it and nothing is sent at it, and l3 stays the last thing between a chain and the ceiling. It is the place kept for a way of pressing that costs a call - a model handed a stretch and answering with what it amounted to - which is the only kind that can say what a stretch came to rather than which parts of it were dropped. Nullable because the levels above it are not: a level nobody has filled in has to be distinguishable from one filled in with keep

tables.name: press
tables._: One row = one compressed form of one stretch of context, one column per level, each naming a row in that level's table: l1 is the least compressed, and the last column that msg_part has been filled in for is the most. Which level goes out is decided per request - the engine counts the bytes it is about to send, and drops a level at a time while it is over api.compress_at. Levels are columns rather than rows because a unit has all three at once, and a lookup that had to scan for 'the l2 row of this unit' would be one join deeper on the hottest path there is. Empty in a column = that level has not been made; the caller falls back to the level below it, and to the raw messages if none exist

columns.name: id
columns._: What task_{mode}.press points at. The kernel does not mint these: whoever writes a level decides, and a hash of the content is what makes two units that compress to the same thing land on the same row without anyone comparing them

columns.name: l1
columns._: -> press_l1.id

columns.name: l2
columns._: -> press_l2.id

columns.name: l3
columns._: -> press_l3.id

columns.name: l4
columns._: -> press_l4.id. Empty for as long as msg_part says nothing about that level

tables.name: press_l1
tables._: The least compressed level. Several rows of press may name the same row here - that is the point: one line standing in for a stretch of units. Whoever reads it takes such a row once, not once per unit that points at it.

columns.name: body
columns._: The text that goes out in place of those messages

columns.name: bytes
columns._: How big body is. Written down because the decision to drop a level is made by adding these up, and reading every body to measure it is the work being avoided

tables.name: press_l2
tables._: The middle level. Same shape as press_l1; a level is a table rather than a column on one table so that a stretch compressed at one level is one row, and the rows of different levels do not have to line up.

tables.name: press_l4
tables._: The fourth level. Nothing is written here yet: msg_part.l4 is empty, which is what says the level is not set up. It exists so that the level after the last one is a column that is already there rather than a migration - the one it is kept for is the way of pressing that costs a call, and that one arrives as a handle, from outside, on a running database. Same shape as the other three.

tables.name: press_l3
tables._: The heaviest level that is set up - as things stand, the last thing between a chain and the ceiling. Same shape as the others.

templates._: Task sub-tables: one per mode present in the cycle table.

columns.name: node
columns._: Which tree node this unit belongs to. **Only a tree-shaped mechanism has nodes**: there a node is a whole attempt, several units stitched together and closed by the one that gets a terminal status. A single-chain mechanism has no attempts to tell apart, so every unit of it stays node 1 - the column is there, it just has nothing to say. Recorded rather than derived: deriving it means walking the parent chain and hard-coding which cycle closes a node, which is wrong the moment the mechanism changes, and wrong without an error.

columns.name: status
columns._: Terminal status: reached / dead_failed / dead_below_bar. Fixed once written, never revised; empty = still running

columns.name: press
columns._: -> press.id: what this unit says in compressed form, at each level that is set up. Empty = nothing has been compressed for it, so it goes out as its messages. One row per unit rather than one per node, because the chain is what grows: a station's messages are on the chain of every station after it, and a run that measured 4136k bytes on one chain had 65 to 86 percent of it in replayed reasoning. A reference rather than the text itself, so that several units can share one compressed line - and written down rather than derived at send time, because derived, the same unit compresses differently on every request, and a context that changes underneath a model is a bug nobody can reproduce

templates._: Agent context tables: one per agent in the agent table.

columns.name: task
columns._: -> task.id. Empty for an instance a user registered but has not assigned work to yet; anything unregistered does not count as existing

templates._: Agent message tables, expanded from the context table. They hold the full context, not only the half that gets pushed out.

columns.name: thought
columns._: What the model thought before it spoke (reasoning_content). It lives here and deliberately NOT in body, because body is what gets replayed: some gateways refuse an assistant message that carries reasoning back, and the replay path has always worked. Recording it costs that path nothing and buys the only account of how an answer was arrived at. Empty for any row no thinking model produced.

columns.name: prompt_tokens
columns._: Tokens sent, TOTALLED over every round this row took. A cut-off answer is continued by asking again with what was said so far, and each round bills its own prompt - so on a continued row this is the sum, not the length of any one prompt. Read it as what the input cost, never as how long the context was: one measured row billed 17232 against a conversation of about 1600 tokens, and a later row can come in lower than an earlier one simply because it was not continued. Null on any row that did not come from a model call.

columns.name: completion_tokens
columns._: Every token the model produced. This INCLUDES the thinking - reasoning_tokens is a part of this number, not a second number to add to it. Subtract to get what was actually spoken.

columns.name: reasoning_tokens
columns._: How much of completion_tokens was thinking. This is the column that says where the wall-clock went. One run averaged 174s per model call while the text that came back averaged some 350 tokens - two tokens a second, which no model is; the gap was thinking, and with no column for it that could only be inferred, never shown. A run that cannot say what it spent cannot say whether its time limit was fair.

columns.name: cached_tokens
columns._: How many of prompt_tokens the vendor served from its own cache. Kept apart from prompt_tokens because the two are priced differently, and a bill nobody can reconstruct is a bill nobody can dispute.
